terms.def: A KMSC staff member at a site, responsible for a set of phones, one operator for every ten phones. The operator hands out the phones, restarts them, and manages the wearers.
The person who wears the phone and records the video, either a site employee or a worker we recruited. Every wearer passes onboarding screening.
The set of sites that one Portfolio Manager owns. Each portfolio has a monthly hour target.
The setup day at a new site, before official filming starts. We set up the stations, labels, and network, give the orientation, and make the pilot recordings.
One recording period of 30 minutes. The collection app stops at 30 minutes, then the phone is restarted and the next cycle starts.
The online form the site lead submits by 6:00 PM, one per site, direct and partner. It goes into the company database, and the company report builds itself from it.
The page that adds up every site's evening check-out. At 6:15 PM the chase list of missing sites goes to Mano. At 8:00 PM the number posts on its own.

The senior operator on a floor with 20 or more phones. Reports to the Portfolio Manager. Does the 7:00 AM count with the Portfolio Manager, runs the floor between visits, and submits the evening check-out by 6:00 PM. A partner site has one too.
A review note on one video, either feedback or fraud. Feedback means something to fix, and fraud means the video is not paid, a penalty, and a possible ban.
A warning on an account. Two strikes pause the phone until the worker is retrained.
The unique ID of one recorded video in the export. QC uses it to link a flag to one video.
The record that shows who wore which phone on which shift.
Footage recorded but not uploaded yet, measured in device-days. More than one day at a site is an incident.
A place with a fast internet line. We bring the phones to the hub, and they upload overnight. One is live, at the Central Cairo warehouse. More hubs are an open decision.
The checklist that every wearer completes before a phone goes on their head.
The daily meeting of Adham, Moharam, and Mano.
Thirty minutes every day when any operator can talk directly to leadership.
A performance improvement plan that lasts 7 days. It comes with a written warning.
If you bring us a site contract, you get 10% on that contract. If you refer a person and we hire them, you get 2,000 EGP.
Any place where people expect more privacy than usual. We never film there.

ownership: Mano owns this map and approves every change. Every edit gets one changelog line with a version and a date.

changelog.text: The evening check-out asks for the number the site already counts. Three days of deriving a day from minutes all time and minutes saved locally ended with every site wrong by a different amount, because the two are read at different moments at different sites, from midday to the next noon, and the bad videos are deleted before the reading at some and after it at others. So the ledger now asks, per phone, for the minutes it recorded today once the bad videos are deleted, which is what the site adds up by hand every night, and the day is that column added up. Minutes saved locally stays as the pending figure. Minutes all time is not asked for: nobody was sure what it was. Days from before this change keep the hours they had, and 16 September carries the hand counts.

A day's hours are everything the phone has, now against last night. Footage lands in minutes saved locally when it is shot and moves to minutes all time when it reaches a hub, and the phones upload overnight, so the rise in minutes all time is last night's upload, which is the day before's filming. Counting a day that way ran a day behind and missed everything still on the phone. The day is now the rise in the two added together, and the overnight upload cancels out of it. A phone whose tag has never been read at that site before is taken to have arrived empty, so what it is holding is what it shot today, and the site's row says how many of its phones were new that night: where the tags change every night the hours cannot be followed phone by phone.

The morning check-in stops counting phones and the day stands on two numbers. The check-in asks four things and nothing else: what time recording started, how many phones are recording, how many are down, and how many employees are present, which is the opt-in rate and the form works it out while you type. The phone readings belong to the evening check-out, which is the only place a phone is read now. Hours recorded today is the rise in a phone's minutes all time since its last check-out, and hours pending upload is what it is still holding tonight. A phone on its first check-out records nothing, because its minutes all time are its whole life and there is nothing to count from. Both numbers are added up per site, per channel and for the day, and they lead the page beside the phones, the hours a phone and the opt-in rate.

The company report and the dashboard are one page. The day opens with what happened and the four numbers it is judged by, then the map, where every business is a single dot carrying its phone count: click it and that business opens, fanning out into its phones on the map and listing them under it. Then the businesses themselves, one card each with the morning, the evening, the hours and the phones, and a card at the foot that adds the day up. The month, the incidents and the notes follow, and the morning and evening numbers, the thirty day charts and the site against site charts are folded under the page. The map only draws the businesses that are running, it reads whatever day you pick, and it is drawn softer than it was.

One count for the phones, and a shorter company report. The two forms no longer ask anybody to type how many phones are out: the list of phones is the count, so the company report and the dashboard read the same number from now on. Where an older day still disagrees, the dashboard says so on the site. The report itself is in reading order now: what happened, what needs attention, four numbers, the month, then every site with a foot that adds up each channel and the day. The morning and the evening number by number, the thirty day charts, and the site against site charts are folded away under the page for whoever wants them.

The dashboard adds up. Six numbers sit above the map now: the red, yellow, and green counts, the hours a day the whole fleet records, the hours one phone records a day, and the hours still sitting on the phones that nobody can use yet. They count every phone, including the ones at a site the map cannot place. Open a site and its phone list ends in a total row: that site's hours a day, its hours today, and the minutes its phones are holding, said in hours underneath.

No page asks for a code any more. The company report, the dashboard, the site database, the team, the incidents, the accounts page and the live editor all open by themselves for the account whose work they are. A page that is not for your account says so and gives you a way to sign in as somebody else, with nothing to type. The shared code stays behind the scenes as a spare key for the scripts, and it is a manager's key: the accounts page and the settings take an account and nothing else.

Who reads what, rebuilt around the account. The map is cut into thirteen sections and each role opens a set of them, and only a founder opens all of them. Money and the risk register left the numbers section for their own. A work email on the team list is what lets a person make an account: it opens by itself, at that person's role, the first time they sign in, and setting them to not active closes it again. My sites is the new page for a person who runs sites: their own sites, what is done today and what is still missing. The three site forms still ask for no account and no code, and when the person filling one in is signed in the form stops asking who they are.

Accounts. Everything except the three site forms is behind a sign-in. A new account waits with no role and opens nothing until management gives it one on the accounts page, and the role decides which sections open. The content of the map is no longer served from the web server, apart from the navigation and the address of the database: the pages read the rest from the database, which answers for the reader's role only. Every page carries the reader's name and the time, faintly on screen and darker on paper. Asking to print, asking to save the page, the Print Screen key, the developer tools, a screen capture, and a copy of a whole page are logged and sent to Slack and to the report email as they happen. A PostHog key on the company report page sends the same events to PostHog.

The dashboard: a map of Egypt drawn in code with every phone as a dot at its site, green from 5 hours a day, yellow from 3, red under 3, grey with no evening reading yet. The hours come from the morning check-ins and the evening check-outs over the last 7, 14, or 30 days. A site sits on it by a map pin from the site database, else by its city. Under the map, one card per site opens on that site's phones.

The site database, once the site registry: every site is Direct or Partner, every site has a Portfolio Manager (a partner puts their own name), Direct sites also have a site lead, and the hub areas are the three Cairo areas, Alexandria, Mansoura, New Mansoura, and Damietta. The morning check-in has a phones active box. The check-ins no longer repeat a partner's name after the site. Form fields sit level with each other. On the org chart the seats being hired are green, and the Recruiters seat is off it.

The company report is boxes and charts: the morning and the evening as rows of numbers, six charts for the last 30 days (hours per day with uploaded and still on the phones, phones filming against employees present, hours per phone, opt-in rate, sites in, morning against evening), four charts by site, and a by-team table. On both forms the phone is picked from a list of 1 to 270, a phone cannot be listed twice, the phones a site used are offered again on the same device, and the evening check-out starts from the morning's list. The morning check-in now takes the same ledger: every phone with its minutes all time and the minutes still on it.

The company report is rebuilt around five numbers: phones active, hours, hours per phone, opt-in rate, and present against filming, each with its last 30 days. Under them a headline in plain words, the sites that need attention tonight, the month as a ring and thirty bars with a projection, hours and present against filming by site, and one week strip per site. It goes out by email every evening once a Resend key and an address are saved. Job postings say less about the work and more about the company. The org chart draws founders as filled seats, opens seats role first, and marks the external agent on its own. Wide trees scroll instead of shrinking. A formatting pass across the site.

The daily report is now the evening check-out: employees present, phones deployed and down, and a ledger with one row per phone, its tag, minutes all time, and minutes still saved on it. The day's hours come from the rise in each phone's all-time minutes. The morning check-in asks for phones recording and employees present, and no longer asks for a channel, scheduled wearers, or a team code. A Head of People and Compliance, hiring now, sits under Mano with the Recruiters.

The org chart has two views, Today and At scale, sized for 25,000 hours now and 500,000 hours in December. Every box is filled, hiring now with its month, or planned. Planned seats and a headcount by month strip show at scale only. Ahmed Alaa is Finance Manager and reports to Adham. Youssef Medhat is Director of Quality Control. The IT Manager seat is now the IT Manager, a priority hire. Recruiters replace the Head of Recruiting, legal stays with outside counsel, and the sourcing agent in China is an external role. Payment questions go to the Finance Manager, device and upload issues to the IT Manager after the Portfolio Manager.

Two new seats, hiring now: a Head of Legal under Adham, who owns every contract, filing, and legal question with the law firm, and a Head of Talent Acquisition under Mano, who fills every open seat and keeps the bench at 10%. Both on the chart, each with a job page. The org chart shrinks a little to fit a wide row instead of cutting it off.

Live edits that work everywhere: the management code and the name are asked in a box on the page, never in a browser dialog. In edit mode every section has a small bar to move it up or down, hide it, or delete it, for everyone, with a Show again to bring it back. Buttons and diagram text open the same box. The Edits page lists section changes with Undo and a Done in the source button. The single-file copy's Edit button opens the same page on the live site.

A Commercial Director seat, hiring now, that vets, signs, walks, and closes every site and faces its owners. Mazen is the Planning and Logistics Lead, with an Inventory Manager under him. An IT Manager runs the phone manager. The process page shows the procedures for every step and gains the vetting rules, the talking points, the site visit checklist, consent through Ahmed Alaa, a weekly audit, and closing an engagement. A Systems page. Open decisions on the overview. One hub until the hub decision is made.

One database behind every form. A team directory feeds the name lists on the evening check-out, the new morning check-in by 9:00 AM, and the incident form, which is now online. The site registry links each site to its Portfolio Manager and site lead and shows the site's own history. The company report shows who started, who reported, the incidents filed, and an activity log, and management closes incidents on their own page. The Slack posts gain the 9:15 AM morning list. Every time is written the same way, the small labels are sentence case, and the procedure headings, the job tables, and the paper forms are tidied.

A Planning and Logistics Lead under Moharam owns the dispatch schedule, the store, the two hubs, the runners, the lines, and the gear. Mano keeps recruiting, papers, wearer files, and this map. A site lead on every floor with 20 or more phones. The evening check-out is an online form, sent by the site lead by 6:00 PM, and the company report builds itself. Two hubs, Central and East. No HR seat and no business development seat. Month end pays on our own audit, then invoices the client.

Jobs: one page per role with the handbook, the posting for job boards, and the offer letter. Uploading rewritten around two ways to upload and three hubs. The company name is gone from every page. Procedures are grouped by role. The capacity calculator splits direct operations from delivery partners. The legal calendar is gone. Every page was cut shorter and simpler, in English and Arabic. Print buttons work inside the preview.

Rebuilt the map as a site, with every section on its own page and the content in JSON files. Added channels, incident playbooks, training, metrics, risks, the never list, the letter generator, the capacity calculator, six more manual subsystems, Arabic for the pages workers use, and print styles.

The whole map on one page: the people, who to call, the nine-stage workflow, the working day, the rules, onboarding screening, the glossary, and the first two manual subsystems, data logistics and asset control.
